source: Photon energy, the fastest electrons and the stopping voltage.
Students think brighter light gives faster electrons.

The photoelectric effect shows light arriving in packets. Each electron gets the energy of one photon, as in The Photoelectric Effect; what is left after the work function becomes its kinetic energy. Each problem here is one short scene and a chain of questions. Answer them in order: each later question uses what you found before, so a slip early on carries through. Keep full precision between steps and round only at the end.
$$E = hf = \frac{hc}{\lambda}, \quad hc = 1240\ \text{eV·nm}; \qquad K_{\max} = E - \phi; \qquad eV_s = K_{\max}.$$ Brighter light means more photons, so more electrons, but not faster ones.
Each wavy packet is one photon. The slowing voltage turns the electrons back; only those with enough energy reach the collector.
Light of $300\ \text{nm}$ falls on potassium ($\phi = 2.3\ \text{eV}$). Find (1) the photon energy, (2) $K_{\max}$ and (3) the stopping voltage.

Expecting brighter light to give faster electrons. The energy each electron gets depends only on the photon, so on the wavelength. Check: below the threshold frequency, no brightness gets any electron out.
